steps.content: Traditional programming: rules + data = answers. Machine Learning: data + answers = rules. ML algorithms learn patterns from data to make predictions on new data. Instead of writing explicit if/else rules, you show examples and the model learns the mapping.

Key terms: Features (input variables), Labels/Targets (output to predict), Training data (examples with labels), Test data (unseen data for evaluation), Model (learned function), Inference (making predictions). ML is a subset of AI focused on learning from data.

steps.question: In ML, what do we call the input variables?
steps.explanation: Features are the input variables (columns) used to make predictions. Labels/targets are the outputs we want to predict.

steps.question: The data used to train a model is called ______ data.
steps.explanation: Training data contains examples with known labels. The model learns from this. Test/validation data is held out for evaluation.

steps.question: Order the typical ML workflow steps
steps.explanation: Data first, then split, model selection, training, evaluation, deployment.

steps.question: Machine Learning requires explicit programming of rules for each decision.
steps.explanation: ML learns patterns from data automatically. You provide examples (data + answers), the algorithm discovers the rules.

steps.question: What is the purpose of test data?
options: To evaluate model performance on unseen data
steps.explanation: Test data is NEVER used during training. It simulates real-world unseen data to estimate how the model will perform in production.

steps.content: Supervised learning: training data has labels (answers). Algorithm learns mapping from features to labels. Tasks: classification (discrete labels: spam/not spam) and regression (continuous: house price). Examples: linear regression, decision trees, neural networks.

Unsupervised learning: training data has NO labels. Algorithm finds structure/patterns on its own. Tasks: clustering (group similar: customer segments), dimensionality reduction (compress features), anomaly detection. Examples: K-means, PCA.

steps.question: Which is a supervised learning task?
steps.explanation: Predicting house prices is regression (continuous target) - supervised. Segmentation, anomalies, compression are unsupervised.

steps.question: Grouping similar data points without labels is called ______.
steps.explanation: Clustering finds natural groups in unlabeled data. K-means is a popular algorithm.

steps.question: Order to classify emails as spam/not spam
steps.explanation: Supervised classification: labeled data -> features -> train -> predict.

steps.question: In unsupervised learning, you evaluate using accuracy against true labels.
steps.explanation: Unsupervised learning has NO true labels. Evaluation uses internal metrics (silhouette score, inertia) or downstream task performance.

steps.question: Which algorithm is commonly used for clustering?
steps.explanation: K-Means partitions data into K clusters by minimizing within-cluster variance. It's the classic unsupervised clustering algorithm.

lessons.title: Model Evaluation
lessons.description: Measure how well your model works

steps.content: Classification metrics: Accuracy (correct/total), Precision (TP/(TP+FP)), Recall (TP/(TP+FN)), F1-score (harmonic mean). Confusion matrix shows TP/FP/TN/FN. ROC-AUC measures ranking ability. Regression metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R².

Train/test split: typically 80/20 or 70/30. Cross-validation: k-fold splits data k times, trains k models, averages scores. Overfitting: model memorizes training data, fails on test (high train accuracy, low test). Underfitting: too simple, fails on both. Regularization prevents overfitting.

steps.question: What does precision measure?
options: Of all positive predictions, how many are correct
Of all actual positives, how many were found
steps.explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP). Of the items we predicted as positive, how many actually are? High precision = few false alarms.

steps.question: The harmonic mean of precision and recall is the ______ score.
steps.explanation: F1 = 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall). Balances precision and recall when you need a single number.

steps.question: Order to calculate accuracy from confusion matrix values
steps.explanation: Accuracy = (true positives + true negatives) / total predictions.

steps.question: High accuracy always means a good model.
steps.explanation: Accuracy can be misleading with imbalanced data. 99% negative class: predicting all negative gives 99% accuracy but 0% recall for positive class.

steps.question: What indicates overfitting?
options: Low training accuracy, high test accuracy
High training accuracy, low test accuracy
steps.explanation: Overfitting = model memorizes training data (high train acc) but doesn't generalize (low test acc). Gap between train and test performance.

lessons.title: Linear Regression
lessons.description: Predict continuous values with a line

steps.content: Linear regression models relationship between features and continuous target as a straight line (or hyperplane). Equation: y = wx + b (simple) or y = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + b (multiple). Goal: find weights (w) and bias (b) that minimize prediction error.

Loss function: Mean Squared Error (MSE) = average of (prediction - actual)². Optimization: Gradient Descent iteratively adjusts weights to minimize loss. Learning rate controls step size. Assumptions: linear relationship, independent errors, homoscedasticity, normal residuals.

steps.question: What does the 'linear' in linear regression refer to?
options: Linear relationship between features and target
steps.explanation: Linear regression assumes the target is a linear combination of features: y = w·x + b. The model is linear in parameters.

steps.question: The loss function commonly used in linear regression is ______.
steps.explanation: MSE = mean((y_pred - y_true)²). Squared errors penalize large mistakes more. Differentiable for gradient descent.

steps.question: Order to implement gradient descent step for linear regression
steps.explanation: Predict -> compute errors -> compute gradient -> update weights. X.T @ errors gives gradient for weights.

steps.question: Linear regression can only model straight lines.
steps.explanation: With feature engineering (polynomial features: x, x², x³), linear regression can model curves. It's linear in PARAMETERS, not necessarily in raw features.

steps.question: What does the learning rate control in gradient descent?
steps.explanation: Learning rate (alpha) scales the gradient step: new_weight = weight - learning_rate * gradient. Too large = overshoot, too small = slow convergence.
